title: Chapter 6: Introduction to Autonomic Pharmacology
authors: Todd W. Vanderah; Bertram G. Katzung

about: Functionally, the nervous system can be divided into two major subdivisions: autonomic and somatic. The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is largely independent (autonomous) in that its activities are not under direct conscious control. It is concerned primarily with control and integration of visceral functions necessary for life such as cardiac output, blood flow distribution, and digestion. By using drugs that mimic or block the actions of chemical transmitters, we can selectively modify many autonomic functions.
sections: Anatomy of the Autonomic Nervous System (sympathetic sacral outflow box)
Neurotransmitter Chemistry of the Autonomic Nervous System (cholinergic transmission, adrenergic transmission, neurotransmitter uptake carriers, cotransmitters)
Functional Organization of Autonomic Activity (central integration, integration of cardiovascular function, presynaptic regulation, postsynaptic regulation)
Pharmacologic Modification of Autonomic Function (Pharmacology of the Eye box)
read_for: 'Anatomy of the Autonomic Nervous System' and Figure 6-1: sympathetic (thoracolumbar) vs parasympathetic (craniosacral) divisions, pre-/postganglionic fibers, adrenal medulla as modified ganglion (10/1).
'Neurotransmitter Chemistry': cholinergic vs noradrenergic fibers; the five drug-target steps - synthesis, storage, release, termination of action, receptor effects (10/1).
'Cholinergic Transmission' (Figure 6-3): choline transporter, ChAT, VAT, VAMPs/SNAPs, acetylcholinesterase - backs 10/5-10/6 cholinergic lectures.
'Adrenergic Transmission' (Figures 6-4, 6-5): tyrosine hydroxylase (metyrosine), VMAT (reserpine), NET (cocaine, antidepressants), MAO/COMT - backs 10/6-10/7 adrenergic lectures.
Table 6-2 'Major autonomic receptor types': M1-M5, Nn/Nm, alpha1/alpha2, beta1-3, D1/D2 with locations and results of ligand binding.
Table 6-3: direct effects of sympathetic vs parasympathetic activity on organ systems (eye, heart, vessels, bronchioles, GI, GU, metabolic).
Table 6-5 'Steps in autonomic transmission: Effects of some drugs' - the one-table map of where each drug class acts.
beyond_lecture: Sympathetic Sacral Outflow box (reclassification of pelvic cholinergic outflow).
NANC neurons, enteric nervous system (Figure 6-2) and cotransmitters (Table 6-1).

peripheral ANS fibers that synthesize and release acetylcholine; these include all preganglionic efferent autonomic fibers and the somatic motor fibers to skeletal muscle, plus most parasympathetic postganglionic and some sympathetic postganglionic fibers.
most postganglionic sympathetic fibers, which work by releasing norepinephrine (noradrenaline).
VAMPs (vesicle-associated membrane proteins) and SNAPs (synaptosomal nerve-associated proteins), which align vesicles with release sites and participate in triggering the release of transmitter.

carries norepinephrine and similar molecules back into the cell cytoplasm from the synaptic cleft; also called uptake 1; inhibited by cocaine, solriamfetol, and certain antidepressant drugs.

nerve fibers in autonomic effector tissues that do not show the histochemical characteristics of either cholinergic or adrenergic fibers; peptides are the most common transmitters, with nitric oxide synthase and purines also present.

early investigators called the parasympathetic system trophotropic (leading to growth), used to 'rest and digest', and the sympathetic system ergotropic (leading to energy expenditure), activated for 'fight or flight'.
